papers.title: A persistent-current-biased and current-actuated switch for superconducting circuits
papers.abstract: Broadband and low-loss superconducting switches can facilitate large-scale quantum information processors and cryogenic detectors by dynamically reconfiguring the connectivity of their circuits. The time dependent connectivity is enabled by the nonlinearity of lossless Josephson junctions, which are often wired into superconducting loops to be controlled by magnetic flux. However, this approach needs a power-consuming constant flux bias and dynamic flux actuation, both of which are hard to isolate from other switches or flux sensitive elements, limiting their integration density. Here, we design and characterize a microwave switch that implements a persistent current bias and direct current actuation to reduce static power consumption, actuation energy and potential crosstalk to other devices. We show that persistent current associated with tens of flux quanta is stable and long-lived, reducing the need for on-the-fly tuning. We further demonstrate that our switch has desirable performance for superconducting-circuit-based quantum information processing, including an off mode with more than 20 dB isolation comparable to commercial ferrite isolators, power handling larger than 100 pW sufficient for resonator readout tones and amplifier pumps, and modulation bandwidth broader than 600 MHz useful for multiplexing schemes.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates a superconducting switch based on an inductive Wheatstone bridge of tunable rf-SQUID inductors, controlled via a persistent current bias and direct current actuation rather than flux threading. The switch achieves >20 dB isolation over 1.9 GHz bandwidth, handles >100 pW power, and exhibits >600 MHz modulation bandwidth suitable for large-scale quantum processors.
summary.motivation: Flux-biased Josephson junction switches require power-consuming constant bias and dynamic flux actuation that are difficult to isolate from nearby devices, limiting integration density. A persistent current bias with DC actuation could reduce static power, crosstalk, and simplify operation in large quantum systems.
summary.method: An inductive bridge with four arms of $N=20$ antisymmetric rf-SQUID arrays (with $\beta = L_{\mathrm{sh}}/L_J = 1.2$) enables orthogonal current patterns for input (X mode), output (Y mode), actuation ($I_Z$), and persistent bias ($I_C$). A heat-activated aluminum patch with lower $T_C$ allows trapping of discrete flux quanta by dissipating applied current, creating a fully superconducting loop once cooled. The coupling rate follows $g_{XY} \propto \sin(\phi_Z/N)\sin(\phi_C/4N)$.
summary.result: Trapped persistent currents (up to ~34 flux quanta) remain stable with <1% decay per day; single flux jumps occur at ~100 h intervals. The switch achieves 20 dB on/off contrast from DC to 1.9 GHz, 1 dB compression at 200 pW (suitable for readout at ~0.1 pW), and modulation bandwidth exceeding 600 MHz with 2.3% single-trap failure rate.

papers.title: A Non-Foster Superconducting Broadband Matching Network
papers.abstract: The nonlinear inductance of the Josephson junction has enabled the development of a wide range of continuous-variable amplifiers and qubit-based devices with unprecedented sensitivity. We present an alternative use of the Josephson junction in the context of broadband impedance matching. The idea poses a potential solution to a longstanding problem in the field of high energy particle physics. The axion, a compelling candidate for the dark matter, converts to a weak electromagnetic signal at an as-yet unknown frequency. As such, the ideal axion detector does not compromise bandwidth for sensitivity, a trade-off intrinsic to all linear, time-invariant and passive circuits. We propose a circuit that uses a Josephson junction in an impedance matching network to overcome these gain-bandwidth constraints and increase the scan rate of axion searches. The Josephson junction can be biased to exhibit negative inductance capable of canceling geometric inductance similar to a capacitor but across a wider frequency range.

summary.summary: This work presents a Josephson junction-based non-Foster impedance matching network designed to achieve broadband signal matching without the bandwidth-sensitivity tradeoff inherent to passive linear circuits, with application to axion dark matter searches. WRSPICE simulations demonstrate power transfer of $-4$ dB across a 40 MHz band (30–70 MHz) comparable to a high-$Q$ resonant capacitive match at a single frequency, with potential bandwidth extension to $\geq 10$ GHz if circuit models remain valid.
summary.motivation: Axion detectors using lumped-element circuits require high-$Q$ resonators for sensitivity, which restricts bandwidth per Bode-Fano limits and implies scan times of tens of thousands of years to cover the full parameter space. Josephson junctions biased to exhibit negative inductance ($L_J = L_{J,0}\cos\phi$ negative for $\pi/2 < \phi < 3\pi/2$) offer an active non-Foster component to overcome these gain-bandwidth constraints.
summary.method: A superconducting loop containing a Josephson junction with critical current $\sim 1$ µA (zero-phase inductance $L_{J,0} \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-10}$ H) is flux-biased to phase $\phi = \pi$ via external bias coil, yielding negative effective inductance that cancels geometric inductance via mutual coupling ($k = 0.3$) over a wide frequency range; power transfer is modeled in WRSPICE using the RSCJ junction model with 0.7 nF per ampere capacitance.
summary.result: The non-Foster circuit achieves $-4$ dB power transfer (versus $-3$ dB for the ideal matched capacitor) across 30–70 MHz with only 13% output power loss from 30 MHz to 70 MHz, compared to narrowband resonant matching; however, stability degrades on millisecond timescales and requires bias current precision better than $10^{-7}$ (100 ppb), mitigable via periodic bias current pulsing every 0.5 µA at 50 MHz drive.
